intro: When two verbs come together, the second one is either an -ing form (I enjoy cooking) or to + base verb (I want to cook). The first verb decides, so you need to learn the most common ones.
objectifs: Use -ing after enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, suggest, keep, practise, can't stand…
Use to + verb after want, would like, decide, hope, plan, need, learn, forget…
Know that like, love, hate, start, begin can take both forms.
Use -ing after a preposition (good at cooking, before leaving) and build want / ask / tell + someone + to.

texte: After these verbs, the second verb takes the -ing form. Many of them talk about likes, habits, or an action that is already happening or that you think about.

The most common is “enjoy”: I enjoy swimming. Never say “I enjoy to swim”. Other very useful verbs: finish, mind (be unhappy about: Do you mind waiting?), avoid, suggest, keep (continue, not stop), practise, miss (feel sad because something is not there), imagine, can't stand (hate), give up (stop).
exemples: I enjoy reading in the evening.
Have you finished cleaning the kitchen?
Do you mind opening the window?
I miss living near the sea.
sections.note: “Suggest” takes -ing (She suggested going to the cinema), never “to”: don't say “She suggested to go”.

texte: After these verbs, the second verb is the infinitive with “to”. Many of them talk about wishes, decisions, plans or efforts for the future.
The most common: want, would like (lesson 34), need, hope, plan, decide, learn, agree, promise, refuse, offer, forget, manage (succeed after trying), try, afford (have enough money for), seem.

lignes: I'd like to book a table.
We decided to stay at home.
I hope to see you soon.
Don't forget to call your mother.
Did you manage to find the hotel?
We can't afford to buy a car.

sections.note: Put “not” before “to” for the negative: I decided not to go.

texte: After like, love, hate, prefer, start, begin, continue, you can use -ing or to with almost no change in meaning: I like swimming / I like to swim. It started raining / It started to rain.

British nuance: “like + -ing” is more about enjoyment (I like dancing); “like + to” is more about a habit you choose because it is useful (I like to arrive early). In American English, “like to” is very common for both.
Be careful: “would like”, “would love”, “would hate”, “would prefer” ALWAYS take to: I'd love to come (not “I'd love coming”).
exemples: I love cooking. / I love to cook.

texte: After a preposition (in, at, of, about, for, without, before, after, by…), a verb is always in the -ing form.
Very common expressions: be good at, be interested in, be afraid of, be tired of, think about, look forward to (here “to” is a preposition!), thank you for, how about…? / what about…?
exemples: I'm looking forward to seeing you.
How about going to the beach?

texte: With want, would like, ask, tell, help, expect, you can put a person between the two verbs: verb + object + to + base verb. Say “I want you to come”. Never say “I want that you come”.
Negative: tell someone not to do something.
exemples: My boss asked me to stay late.
The doctor told him not to smoke.
sections.note: Some verbs (stop, remember, forget, try) change meaning with the form: stop smoking (not smoke any more) / stop to smoke (stop doing something else so you can smoke). You will study this in lesson 113 (B1).

formule: enjoy / finish / mind / avoid / suggest / keep + -ing · want / need / decide / hope / learn / forget + to + verb · preposition + -ing · want someone to…
prononciation: “to” before a verb is weak: /tə/ (I want to go /aɪ ˈwɒnt tə ˈɡəʊ/). In informal speech: “wanna” (want to), “gonna” (going to). Understand them, but don't write them.
“I'd like to” sounds like /aɪd ˈlaɪk tə/: the d of “I'd” is light but present.
-ing is /ɪŋ/, with no hard g at the end.
“Do you mind…?”: stress MIND; the voice goes up at the end. A polite answer: “No, not at all” (= it's no problem).
“look forward to”: stress FOR-: /lʊk ˈfɔːwəd tə/.
erreurs: She suggested to take a taxi.
I'm interested to learn English. (meaning: it interests me)
Before to leave, close the door.
I'm looking forward to see you.
I'm looking forward to seeing you.
In look forward to, “to” is a preposition: -ing.

dialogue.contexte: Two friends in Québec talk about their summer plans.
lignes: Have you decided to go anywhere this summer?
Yes! I want to visit Vancouver. I enjoy travelling by train, so I'm planning to take the train across Canada.
A bit. I can't afford to stay in hotels, so I'm thinking about staying with friends.
Good idea. I'd love to come with you, but I need to work in July.
What about meeting me there in August?
Maybe! I don't mind flying. I'll ask my boss to give me a week off.
Great! Don't forget to tell me. I'm really looking forward to seeing the mountains!

mots: I enjoy walking in the forest.
be unhappy or annoyed about something
give an idea for others to think about
They decided to move to Ghent.
I hope to pass the exam.
I managed to fix my bike.
We can't afford to travel this year.
say that you will certainly do something
I'm looking forward to the holidays.
feel happy about something that will happen

items: She wants (to buy / buying) a new phone.
He hopes (to find / finding) a job soon.
Do you mind (to close / closing) the door?

exercices.consigne: Put the verb in brackets in the right form (-ing or to + verb).
Rewrite the sentence with want / ask / tell + person + to.
items: My mother says: “Paul, clean your room.” (tell)
My mother tells Paul to clean his room.
I say to you: “Please help me.” (ask)
I'm asking you to help me.
The teacher tells us not to talk.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I want that you call me.
I want you to call me.
I'm looking forward to meet you.
I'm looking forward to meeting you.
We can't afford going on holiday.
We can't afford to go on holiday.

exercices.consigne: Use the words to write a correct sentence.
items: She learnt to drive last year. / She learned to drive last year.
I / would like / you / come / with me
I'd like you to come with me.

exercices.consigne: Write five true sentences: something you enjoy doing, something you want to do, something you avoid, something you are good at, and a plan (plan / hope).
items: I enjoy cooking for my friends. I want to learn the guitar. I avoid driving in Brussels at rush hour. I'm quite good at drawing. I'm planning to visit my cousins in Douala next year.

a_retenir: + -ing: enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, suggest, keep, practise, miss, can't stand.
+ to: want, would like, need, hope, plan, decide, learn, forget, manage, afford, promise.
Both: like, love, hate, start, begin (but would like / would love + to).
Preposition + -ing: good at cooking, before leaving, look forward to seeing.
want / ask / tell + person + to: I want you to come (never “want that”).
